sections.Bottom Line: The audited-engagement-harness is a proposed implementation specification for an opt-in, bounded AuditedEngagement mode within Librarian that uses a Manage–Execute–Audit loop.
sections.What It Solves: It addresses the need for long-running, mutation-capable work to be resumable and to require pre-mutation evidence and feasibility checks. It ensures that requirements can be checked against durable, inspectable state and prevents a model from becoming the authority for vault mutations or human decisions.
sections.Claims:
*Origin: source-stated - what the text itself says, part by part.*

- Librarian will add an opt-in, bounded AuditedEngagement mode for work whose requirements can be checked against durable, inspectable state. (part 1)
- AuditedEngagement uses a Manage–Execute–Audit loop but remains one execution mode rather than the default. (part 1)
- The implementation must preserve authority boundaries for the Core, VaultCoordinator, VaultWriter, IndexService, and policy broker. (part 1)
- Goals include making long-running, mutation-capable work resumable and requiring pre-mutation evidence and feasibility checks. (part 1)
- AuditedEngagement is an opt-in session purpose where typed events coordinate requirements, contracts, evidence, audits, and checkpoints. (part 2)
- Session reduction is the deterministic fold of validated Session events that changes requirement status. (part 2)
- Integrity refers to whether work stayed within contract protected targets and audit constraints, separate from semantic correctness. (part 2)
- Six gates, including Host lifecycle and SQLite ownership, are required prerequisites for the system. (part 3)
- Normal sessions, existing macros, and legacy tiers must continue to work through 2.x while gates are completed. (part 3)
- Modes include Standard session, Plan-only engagement, AuditedEngagement, and Workbench-linked AuditedEngagement. (part 3)
- The active Core owns every transition, and all components must use the Core API and its boundaries. (part 4)
- The broker must compute effective authority as the intersection of several factors, including caller permission, role/profile permission ceiling, and session phase. (part 4)
- No component may widen the intersection of effective authority; semantic ranking or Manager recommendations may only select among already eligible options. (part 4)
- A user-authored or user-locked constraint must not be rewritten by a model, though a model may propose a new constraint as a checkpoint option. (part 5)
- An AuditedSubtaskContract is immutable after preflight and requires a new contract if a target, constraint, route, tool bundle, context policy, or state epoch changes materially. (part 5)
- A mutation contract requiring before-state evidence must acquire all required pre-mutation snapshots before its first write. (part 5)
- Policy corrections are typed, bounded, and auditable, and cannot override the constraint ledger. (part 6)
- A state transition is valid only when a durable Session event records the prior state, event type, actor, state epoch, input references, result, and resulting state. (part 6)
- Reduction MAY reach COMPLETED only if every authoritative Requirement has the specified clean verification evidence at the current epoch. (part 6)
- A result must be labelled environment_feasible and cannot be labelled semantically correct, constraint-complete, secure, or guaranteed to succeed. (part 7)
- When a before-state artifact is required, Core captures an EvidenceSnapshot, validates the target's fingerprint and lease, and then the Executor can receive a mutation-capable contract. (part 7)
- A ContextCapsule uses a profile- and route-configurable hard token budget, reserving space for contract fields, target content, evidence, and local context in a specific order. (part 7)
- Work budget controls Core-side turns, action attempts, delegated work, audit work, time, and cost. (part 8)
- Tier A deterministic audit runs after a mutation-capable contract and before Tier B, returning clean, suspect, or violation integrity statuses. (part 8)
- Tier B read-only LLM audit is invoked only after Tier A is clean and requires a fresh audit capsule without raw Executor reasoning. (part 8)
- The invalidation engine follows typed dependency edges to mark dependent records stale or untrusted, preserving original source and historical audit records. (part 9)
- Deterministic rules or human decisions, rather than models, create authoritative invalidation events. (part 9)
- The first implementation should emit deterministic, low-cost signals such as stall, environment drift, evidence coverage, scope mismatch, and optional semantic drift. (part 9)
- Markdown lacking a Librarian shape receives a virtual, root-scoped workspace_document identity for search and context. (part 10)
- A derived-index phase builds a disposable structural graph for adopted Markdown without mutating user files. (part 10)
- Context retrieval prioritizes direct evidence and semantic links, using structural relations as an explainable fallback. (part 10)
- Traces must not contain API keys, secret references, raw provider payloads, hidden reasoning, full prompt text, or browser session credentials. (part 11)
- Evaluated engagements record various metrics including admission outcome, completion status, integrity violations, and resource shares like token, time, and cost. (part 11)
- Cost estimates are considered estimates rather than provider invoices unless reconciled under an explicit accounting policy. (part 11)
- Phase D adds trust-zone labels, evidence-first interrogation cards, and links AuditedEngagement rounds to Workbench records. (part 12)
- Phase E focuses on read-only structural parsing, layered dedupe, and tuning capsule budgets using recorded engagement outcomes. (part 12)
- Phase F requires completing handshake/lifecycle checks, running deterministic L0 and L1–L3 suites, and shipping behind a per-vault feature flag. (part 12)
- AuditedEngagement mutations only occur within active Core, VaultWriter, target lease, and IndexService authority boundaries. (part 13)
- Tier A blocks completion if it detects out-of-scope writes, audit writes, stale target state, or missing deterministic verification. (part 13)
- Untrusted input cannot use its content to gain write, execution, credential, route, or promotion authority in the same episode. (part 13)
- … and 25 more across the text (all kept in the staged item's deep-read record)
sections.Evidence & Limits:
*Origin: source-stated - the limits the source itself states.*

- Proposed implementation specification, not implemented. (part 1)
- Tier B is experimental and non-default until HARNESS-08's go/no-go (§12.3). (part 1)
- Deferred: trust-zone propagation, learned tool selection, graph context, generic behaviour-tree framework, and automatic promotion or route switching. (part 1)
- Non-goals include: autonomous goal expansion, self-authored permanent policies, self-approved promotion, or automatic model failover. (part 1)
- The LongHorizon-Harness loop is optional and does not prove a gain on every task or route. (part 2)
- Do not assume a stronger model always reduces total cost or that a hybrid pairing is superior. (part 2)
- Long task duration alone is not sufficient for admission to the Auditable Closure Gate. (part 2)
- A successful gate does not establish that the task is feasible in a domain sense, that its constraints are complete, or that the anticipated result is correct. (part 3)
- Legacy tiers are a compatibility projection and MUST NOT become a second authority for a live AuditedEngagement route. (part 3)
- A staged research summary normally remains partial or human_judgment unless its exact claim coverage and resolution rule are separately specified. (part 3)
- Tier B audit is experimental (HARNESS-08). (part 4)
- Tier A auditors cannot claim semantic completeness beyond deterministic checks. (part 4)
- Records are logical records and not a separate engagement store or a persistent class per record. (part 4)
- A user-authored or user-locked constraint MUST NOT be rewritten by a model. (part 5)
- The contract is immutable after preflight; changes to targets, constraints, routes, tool bundles, context policy, or state epoch require a new contract. (part 5)
- The contract MUST express a bounded action, not a vague goal. (part 5)
- Policy corrections are not self-modifying model policy and cannot override the constraint ledger. (part 6)
- At most five active corrections MAY be rendered in a capsule. (part 6)
- The Manager does not receive direct vault tools, shell tools, network tools, or raw Executor chat. (part 6)
- The system MUST NOT hash an entire vault to judge audit integrity to avoid false violations for independent documents. (part 7)
- The assembler MUST NOT evict contract facts, target state, or mandatory evidence. (part 7)
- The assembler MUST NOT claim to implement a trained graph-conditioned selector unless one is actually trained, versioned, and qualified. (part 7)
- Model behaviour exposes provider-native thinking only when the exact expectation record and trusted adapter permit them. (part 8)
- Tier A does not infer that an open-ended conclusion is true. (part 8)
- Tier B is experimental and non-default until HARNESS-08's predeclared go/no-go result. (part 8)
- Green signals never prove correctness. (part 9)
- An embedding similarity score, action-loop entropy score, citation-to-claim ratio, or numeric threshold MUST remain advisory until formula version, test corpus, false positive/negative analysis, and profile/route calibration are met. (part 9)
- Labels do not establish that content is true, harmless, user-approved, or safe to execute. (part 9)
- The product adaptation does not claim to reproduce a particular paper's parser, accuracy, memory, or depth result. (part 10)
- Context retrieval begins shallow and expands only under the capsule budget. (part 10)
- Near-duplicate suggestions require human resolution and cannot silently collapse evidence provenance. (part 10)
- The trace MUST NOT contain API keys, secret references, raw provider payloads, hidden reasoning, full prompt text, unrestricted document text, or browser session credentials. (part 11)
- Cost estimates are estimates, not provider invoices, unless reconciled to a provider source under an explicit accounting policy. (part 11)
- This is an implementation map, not authorization to bypass existing contracts. (part 11)
- Poisoned or ambiguous input cannot acquire write/execution authority. (part 12)
- A frontier-lead/open-executor hypothesis is an experiment, not an assumed improvement. (part 12)
- Do not deploy policy changes by inferred traffic splitting. (part 12)
- The specification was informed by a locally supplied corpus and references that do not independently certify a Librarian implementation. (part 13)
- Simulator studies and proxy metrics do not prove a universal prompt or embedding threshold. (part 13)
- Formal/solver verification applies only where the artifact has an appropriate verifier. (part 13)

sections.Bottom Line: This is an application record for the Librarian V2 project that reviews how Claude and Codex use and build the Librarian and delegate to DeepInfra.

sections.Claims:
*Origin: source-stated - what the text itself says, part by part.*

- The project measured how Claude and Codex use and build the Librarian and delegate to DeepInfra, focusing on token usage, quota loss, and resume costs. (part 1)
- Anchored extraction involves a model emitting typed JSON with a verbatim quote and page, where a script verifies the quote exists on that page. (part 1)
- A cheap model asked to rate applicability finds an analogy almost everywhere, meaning the rating does not discriminate. (part 1)
- The research identified various metrics and methods, including drift-propagation equations, constraint-compliance, and selective communication under a budget. (part 1)

- Hosted-model readers differ more than their price suggests, with quote-location ranges from 99.2% to 64.5%. (part 2)

sections.Bottom Line: GraphRAG is a graph-based approach to question answering over private text corpora that uses an LLM to build an entity knowledge graph and pre-generate community summaries.
sections.What It Solves: Conventional vector RAG fails on global sensemaking questions that require a summary of an entire text corpus rather than the retrieval of specific records. GraphRAG addresses this by using map-reduce processing to generate partial responses from community summaries which are then summarized into a final response.
sections.Claims:
*Origin: source-stated - what the text itself says, part by part.*

- RAG fails on global questions directed at an entire text corpus because these are query-focused summarization (QFS) tasks rather than explicit retrieval tasks. (p. 1)
- Prior QFS methods do not scale to the quantities of text indexed by typical RAG systems. (p. 1)
- GraphRAG is a graph-based approach to question answering over private text corpora that scales with question generality and source text quantity. (p. 1)
- Vector RAG works well for queries answered by information in a small set of records but does not support sensemaking queries requiring global understanding of an entire dataset. (p. 2)
- GraphRAG is a graph-based RAG approach that enables sensemaking over the entirety of a large text corpus. (p. 2)
- GraphRAG constructs a knowledge graph, partitions it into a hierarchy of communities, and generates community-level summaries in a bottom-up manner. (p. 2)
- GraphRAG leverages summaries over large sections of data as "self-memory" and generates a graph index to create a thematic partitioning via graph-based community detection. (p. 3)
- GraphRAG uses the inherent modularity of graphs to recursively create increasingly global summaries by using an LLM to summarize the community hierarchy. (p. 3)
- The authors propose an approach for generating questions to evaluate global sensemaking over an entire corpus, rather than explicit fact retrieval. (p. 3)
- The Graph RAG pipeline uses an LLM-derived graph index consisting of nodes, edges, and covariates extracted and summarized by domain-tailored LLM prompts. (p. 4)
- Community detection partitions the graph index into groups that the LLM can summarize in parallel during indexing and query time. (p. 4)
- A global answer is produced via query-focused summarization over all community summaries relevant to a query. (p. 4)
- LLM prompts can be tailored to specific domains by choosing domain-appropriate few-shot exemplars for in-context learning. (p. 5)
- LLMs can be prompted to extract entities, relationships, and claims, which is a form of abstractive summarization. (p. 5)
- Each hierarchy level provides a community partition that covers graph nodes in a mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive way. (p. 6)
- GraphRAG generates community summaries by adding element summaries for nodes, edges, and related claims to a template. (p. 6)
- Algorithm 1 describes a prompting procedure to generate K*N*M high-level questions requiring global understanding of a corpus. (p. 7)
- The procedure prompts an LLM to describe K user personas, identify N tasks per user, and generate M questions per user-task pair. (p. 7)
- Directness is a control criterion that evaluates the concision of an answer and serves as a reference for judging other criteria. (p. 8)
- Directness is effectively in opposition to comprehensiveness and diversity. (p. 8)
- A fixed context window size of 8k tokens was used for generating community and global answers. (p. 9)
- Graph indexing with a 600 token window took 281 minutes for the Podcast dataset. (p. 9)
- All Graph RAG conditions outperformed naïve RAG on comprehensiveness and diversity. (p. 10)
- Conditions C1-C3 showed slight improvements in answer comprehensiveness and diversity over TS. (p. 10)
- For both News and Podcast datasets, global search conditions (C0-C3) and source text summarization (TS) had greater comprehensiveness than vector RAG (SS), with statistically significant differences (p <.05). (p. 11)
- In the Podcast dataset, all global search conditions had significantly greater diversity than SS across all distance thresholds (p<.05). (p. 11)
- GraphRAG combines knowledge graph generation and query-focused summarization to support human sensemaking over entire text corpora. (p. 12)
- Initial evaluations show GraphRAG provides substantial improvements over a vector RAG baseline in answer comprehensiveness and diversity. (p. 12)
- The default GraphRAG initialization pipeline uses GPT-4 prompts for default graph extraction and claim extraction. (pp. 18-19)
- Entity extraction uses a multipart LLM prompt to identify entity names, types, and descriptions, as well as relationships between entities. (pp. 18-19)
- Graph RAG is the winner for Comprehensiveness because it provides a more detailed list from a wider range of entertainment sectors. (p. 20)
- Graph RAG is the winner for Diversity because it covers a varied range of figures and cites specific data sources for each. (p. 20)
- The goal is to identify all entities of specific types from a text document and all relationships among them. (p. 21)
- Step 1 involves identifying entities and extracting their name, type, and a comprehensive description. (p. 21)
- The goal is to write a comprehensive report of a community using a list of entities, their relationships, and optional claims. (p. 22)
- The report informs decision-makers about community information and potential impact, including legal compliance, technical capabilities, and reputation. (p. 22)
- When referencing data, do not list more than 5 record ids in a single reference; use the top 5 most relevant ids and add '+more'. (pp. 24-25)
- Points supported by data should list relevant reports as references using the format [Data: Reports (report ids)]. (pp. 24-25)
- Table 6 presents pairwise comparisons of six conditions on four metrics across 125 questions and two datasets. (p. 26)
- Winning conditions received 100, losing conditions 0, and ties 50, with scores averaged over five evaluation runs. (p. 26)
- … and 50 more across the text (all kept in the staged item's deep-read record)
sections.Evidence & Limits:
*Origin: source-stated - the limits the source itself states.*

- RAG fails on global questions directed at an entire text corpus, such as “What are the main themes in the dataset?”, because this is a query-focused summarization (QFS) task rather than an explicit retrieval task. (p. 1)
- Prior QFS methods do not scale to the quantities of text indexed by typical RAG systems. (p. 1)
- The approach is shown for a class of global sensemaking questions over datasets in the 1 million token range. (p. 1)
- vector RAG works well for queries that can be answered with information localized within a small set of records. (p. 2)
- vector RAG approaches do not support sensemaking queries, meaning queries that require global understanding of the entire dataset. (p. 2)
- The challenge arises when the volume of data requires a RAG approach, since vector RAG approaches are unable to support sensemaking over an entire corpus. (p. 2)
- Longer text chunks require fewer LLM calls but suffer from degraded recall of information that appears early in the chunk. (p. 4)
- Some criteria are generic to vector RAG systems and not relevant to global sensemaking, such as 'context relevance', 'faithfulness', and 'answer relevance'. (p. 4)
- The work lacks a gold standard for evaluation. (p. 4)
- The default prompt extracts the broad class of “named entities” like people, places, and organizations. (p. 5)
- Domains with specialized knowledge (e.g., science, medicine, law) will benefit from few-shot exemplars specialized to those domains. (p. 5)
- In this manuscript, the analysis uses exact string matching for entity matching. (p. 5)
- Leaf-level community element summaries are added to the LLM context window until the token limit is reached. (p. 6)
- Higher-level community summaries are generated by substituting sub-community summaries for longer element summaries if they do not fit within the token limit. (p. 6)
- It is an open question whether a particular level in the hierarchical community structure offers the best balance of summary detail and scope for general sensemaking questions. (p. 6)
- The procedure generates questions that require understanding of the entire corpus and do not require retrieval of specific low-level facts. (p. 7)
- There is a lack of gold standard answers to the activity-based sensemaking questions. (p. 7)
- The evaluation uses a head-to-head comparison approach using an LLM evaluator to judge relative performance. (p. 7)
- Directness is effectively in opposition to comprehensiveness and diversity, so no method is expected to win across all four criteria. (p. 8)
